transcript.content: Hi, welcome in — I'm Dr. [Name]. What brings you in to see me today?

Hi. Well, what brought me in today is that I keep getting up in meetings or at dinner when everyone else is seated. It's... I'll just suddenly feel like I need to get up and refill my coffee, or go check a handout, or just walk to the back of the room. And the thing is, none of it is really urgent. I just can't seem to stay in my seat when I'm supposed to.
Can you tell me when this first started — have you always had trouble sitting still since you were a kid, or is this something new that's developed more recently?

It's not a new thing, no. I've been this way since I was a kid. Even as a young girl, my report cards always said that I was bright, but... well, that I just couldn't stay in my seat or wait my turn. My mother actually used to joke that I wore a path in the floor between my desk and the pencil sharpener before I was even ten years old. So, yes, it's definitely been there my whole life.
Besides the restlessness, do you also struggle with staying focused on tasks, making careless mistakes, or forgetting things in your daily life?

No, not really. I mean, I don't have trouble focusing on my lesson plans or grading papers, and I wouldn't say I make careless mistakes. I'm actually pretty organized. It's really just the physical part... the needing to be up and moving around. I don't feel like I'm forgetful or scattered in my thinking, just restless in my body.
Do you often find yourself interrupting others in conversation or blurting out answers before someone finishes a question?

Yes, I do. In group discussions, I often jump in before someone has actually finished their thought. I notice it a lot at my book club, or... or during our curriculum meetings at school. It's just that the response is already right there in my head, and I end up blurting it out before I can even stop myself.
Would you say these restless and impulsive behaviors cause real problems for you in more than one area of your life — for example, both at work and at home or in your social relationships?

Yes, I would say so. It's... well, it's really started to affect my relationships, both at work and out in my community. Like I mentioned with the curriculum meetings and my book club—people just lose patience with me when I keep interrupting or can't sit still. I can see it on their faces. And then I just end up leaving those gatherings feeling embarrassed, you know, instead of actually feeling connected to anyone.
